**A Love Letter to the Unseen Hours**

The room is always colder than I remember it being. Not the kind of cold that clings to your bones like winter, but the quiet, creeping kind—the kind that seeps in through the cracks in the walls when you least expect it, when you’re not pressing your palm against the windowpane to feel for draughts. It’s the kind of cold that doesn’t announce itself with a shiver but with a slow, insidious numbness, like the way time erodes a memory before you’ve even realized it’s fading. I sat here earlier today, somewhere between noon and twilight, and the light was this strange, watery blue-gray, the kind that makes everything look like it’s underwater. Not the vibrant, living blue of a summer sky, but the dull, metallic sheen of a mercury lamp in a parking lot at midnight. It made the bookshelves look like they were sinking into the floor, their spines warped and leaning as if gravity had finally claimed them.

I wonder sometimes if this is what it means to grow older. Not the wrinkles or the stiff joints—those are just the public parts of aging, the ones that humiliate you in checkout lines and at the gym while you’re trying to adjust your shoelace. No, the real decay is quieter. It’s in the way my coffee doesn’t taste as strong as it used to, not because the café has watered down the espresso, but because my tongue has dulled. It’s in the way a sixty-second ad for a car dealership on TV feels like an eternity now, when once I’d have flipped past it without a thought. It’s in the way I now recognize certain sounds as milestones— the chime of a microwave signaling that my lunch is ready, the *click* of a light switch when I step into a room I swear I’ve stood in a hundred times before, the creak of floorboards that tells me someone is moving through the house even when I know no one is there.

I don’t know if this is nostalgia or just the way a person’s mind starts to fold in on itself as the years accumulate. Maybe it’s both. Maybe nostalgia is just the ghost of a future you never saw coming.

---

I was reading a book the other day—one of those absurdly dense literary novels that demand labor from the reader like a farmer demanding the last of his crop before winter. It was about a man who spends his life collecting broken objects, not because he has a particular affection for any of them, but because he believes that if he can find the right combination of fragments, he’ll stumble upon some greater truth about life. Or maybe it was about a man who was afraid of breaking things himself and so surrounded himself with the wreckages of others as a sort of emotional armor. The prose was so heavy it might as well have been a thousand-page brick wrapped in velvet. I kept falling asleep, not because I was tired, but because it reminded me of my old college philosophy classes, where the professor would drone on about Derrida and the absence of the text and I’d watch the moths batter themselves against the fluorescent lights so brutally that one of them eventually gave up and dropped to the linoleum.

The thing about reading a difficult book is that it makes you feel smart even when you’re not. You float through the sentences like a well-educated specter, nodding sagely at words you don’t fully understand, then sitting back afterward like you’ve just solved a particularly thorny crossword puzzle. But in the gaps between my semi-conscious moments of reading, I found myself thinking about all the things I used to believe in passionately—social justice, the power of art, the idea that if I just read enough and thought deeply enough, I could somehow *earn* the right to be taken seriously by the world. Now they feel like childhood beliefs, like the myth of Santa Claus or the infallibility of teachers. Santa didn’t come this year; teachers lie; art is just another industry; justice is mostly about whoever shouts loudest, like a kindergarten fight over the last juice box.

I don’t know when the disillusionment set in. Maybe it was the day I realized that the people I admired most were also the most quietly cruel. Maybe it was when I stood in a museum looking at a painting that someone had spent years creating, only to have a group of schoolchildren scream past it in twenty minutes because they were being herded like livestock. Maybe it was the first time I Googled a conspiracy theory and, instead of being outraged, I felt a strange, unsettling *relief*—ah, so it’s not that nothing makes sense, it’s that *nothing* makes sense. That’s kind of a relief, actually.

---

The other night, I dreamed I was back in my first apartment, the one with the leaky faucet and the landlord who never fixed anything. It was the first place I lived alone, which at the time felt like a form of freedom, but in the dream felt like a sentence. I was trying to get out of it—I was packing a box, and for some reason, it was filled with old love letters, but instead of being written in ink, they were written in blood. The more I tried to close the box, the more the letters squirmed, their edges dark and damp, bleeding into the cardboard. Then the landlord appeared—average height, average face, the kind of man who could walk past you on the street and in five minutes you wouldn’t remember what he looked like. He leaned against the doorframe and said, “You always thought you were the hero of your own story.” And then he walked away.

I woke up with the taste of metal in my mouth, which I always do when dreams leave a residue like that. The dream felt like a message, but I don’t know if it was from my subconscious or from some external force that was tired of me complaining about my life looking through the wrong end of the telescope. Maybe it’s not that I’m a failure, but that I *knew* I was going to be one all along. Maybe the blood in the letters was from a wound I gave myself.

---

I went to a poetry reading last week. Or maybe it was a performance art piece. It was hard to tell. The poet—a woman with silver braids and a voice like sandpaper—stood on a stage draped in black fabric that might have been a curtain or might have been a shroud. She read a poem that took forty-five minutes to recite, and at the halfway mark, I noticed a man in the front row had fallen asleep and was snoring gently, his head lolling back like a broken doll’s. The poet paused mid-line, and for a second, I thought she might yell at him, or at least glare, but instead she just nodded at the audience and said, “He’s the only one here who knows what matters.” Then she continued.

I don’t remember the poem. I don’t think she did either, not really. Poetry readings are like that—more about the performance than the words. But I remember feeling, just for a second, that if I sat very still and closed my eyes, I could will myself to disappear. Not in some spiritual way, but like a smudge of chalk on a sidewalk erasing itself over time. The way some graffiti fades when the rain comes.

---

They say that the opposite of love is not hate, but indifference. I think that’s true. Indifference is the real death. Hate at least acknowledges that something matters. Indifference is the quiet eraser of everything. It’s what happens when you stop caring if the thing is good or bad, if it’s beautiful or ugly, if it’s even there at all. That’s the cold I was talking about earlier—the cold that doesn’t shiver or ache, but simply is.

I used to think that growing up meant accumulating more meaning, like a tree growing rings, each one greater than the last. But now I think it might be the opposite: every year peels something away. The truer you get, the thinner the skin. Love, ambition, wonder—they’re all just layers, and one day you wake up and you’re standing in the dark without even a shell to protect you.

---

I was walking home from the grocery store the other day, carrying a paper bag that crinkled with every step. It was one of those evening walks where the sky is the color of a bruise, deep purple shifting into something darker, like an old oil slick on pavement. I passed a little girl on a bicycle, no training wheels, her tiny hands gripping the handlebars like she was holding on for dear life. She was riding in the middle of the sidewalk, dangerously close to the curb, and for a second, I thought about warning her—watch out, kid, the street’s not safe—but then she veered off without so much as a swerve, as if she’d known all along that the curb was exactly where she needed to be.

I envied her. Not in a bitter way, but in the way you envy a bird knowing exactly how high to fly so it doesn’t crash into a window. She wasn’t questioning her path. She wasn’t afraid of making the wrong turn or taking a step that wasn’t mathematically proven to lead somewhere. She just *moved*, like the world was hers and there was no other option but to ride through it.

For the first time in years, I felt something like hope—not in a grandiose way, not the kind that makes you want to change the world, but the small, stubborn kind, the kind that says maybe it’s okay that I don’t know where I’m going, as long as I keep pedaling.

---

I think about how strange it is that bodies age, but desires don’t. Or maybe they do, and we just mistake them for something else. The first time I fell in love, it felt like my ribs had been pried open and my heart had been plugged directly into an outlet. Every thought, every breath, was just another surge of electricity through my body. I thought that was the way love would always feel—sharp, electric, impossible to ignore. But now, love feels more like a slow leak. Not the kind that floods the basement and ruins the foundation, but the kind that just quietly fills a space until you don’t notice it’s there anymore. You walk through the room and realize the floor is damp.

I don’t know if that’s maturity or exhaustion. Maybe it’s both.

---

I should probably stop writing now. The page is filling up, and the words are starting to feel like they’re echoing instead of speaking. I could go on—there’s so much more to say about the way time folds in on itself, about the way silence can be louder than sound, about the way a single hair on my chin that refuses to be plucked feels like a personal betrayal. But maybe this is enough. Maybe the point isn’t to say everything, but to say something, even if it’s only a half-truth, even if it dissolves as soon as the ink dries.

So I’ll end with this:

The room is still cold. Not the kind that announces itself, but the kind that’s always there, just beneath the surface, waiting for you to notice it again. And me? I’m still here too, sitting in the quiet, trying to figure out if this is the life I was supposed to live or just the one that happened to fit. Maybe it doesn’t matter. Maybe the only thing that matters is that I’m still typing, still trying, still here at all.

For now, that’s enough.
